IB Computer Science

A1.1 Computer Hardware & Operation

Topic A1: Computer Fundamentals | Inside the CPU

The Big Question

🤔 Your laptop has 8 cores.

Is it always 8× faster than a 1‑core CPU?

❌ Common misconception: “More cores = linear speedup.”

If that were true, doubling cores would always double performance.

✅ Reality: performance depends on parallelisable work,

and on whether the CPU can keep each core fed with data (memory hierarchy) and instructions (pipeline).

What is a CPU?

When you click “Save”, what actually turns that request into electrical actions?

The CPU executes instructions stored in memory.

It repeats the fetch–decode–execute cycle millions/billions of times per second.

To do this efficiently, it uses specialised components and very fast internal storage.

Did you know?

A “3.5 GHz” clock is ~3.5 billion cycles per second (though modern CPUs do more than one thing per cycle).

Most performance losses come from waiting for data to arrive from slower memory levels.

CPU Components (At a Glance)

If the CPU is the “brain”, what are its “parts”?

ALU — arithmetic + logic operations

CU — decodes and co-ordinates execution

Registers — ultra-fast temporary storage

Buses — pathways for data, addresses, control

Why this matters

Exam questions often focus on where data is at each stage of execution.

That means naming the correct register and the correct bus.

🔗 Connection to A1.2: every value in registers is ultimately stored as binary (often displayed to humans in hex).

Registers: the CPU’s “scratchpad”

How can the CPU keep track of “what next?” while executing instructions?

A register is tiny but extremely fast CPU storage.

Some registers store addresses, others store data or the current instruction.

Deep Dive: key registers you must know

Program Counter (PC)

Stores: the memory address of the next instruction.

Why it matters: it defines program order (unless a branch/jump changes it).

Memory Address Register (MAR)

Stores: the address currently being accessed in memory.

Typical flow: PC → MAR during the fetch stage.

Memory Data Register (MDR)

Stores: the data/instruction being transferred to/from memory.

Think: MDR is the “buffer” for memory transfers.

Instruction Register (IR)

Stores: the instruction currently being decoded/executed.

Why it matters: the CU reads the IR to decide what to do next.

Accumulator (AC)

Stores: intermediate results from the ALU.

Example: partial sums in multi-step calculations.

Buses: How Components Communicate

How does the CPU talk to memory without “direct wires” for every location?

Address bus: which location?

Data bus: what data/instruction?

Control bus: what action (read/write/interrupt)?

Width matters

Address bus width limits addressable memory.

Example: a 32-bit address bus can address up to 232 distinct locations.

Typical exam trap

Address bus is usually unidirectional (CPU → memory).

Data bus is typically bidirectional (read + write).

Memory Hierarchy (Speed vs Size)

If RAM is “fast”, why does the CPU still need cache and registers?

Closer to the CPU = faster (but smaller and more expensive).

Hierarchy: Registers → L1 → L2 → L3 → RAM

Cache hit = fast. Cache miss = stall.

Onion analogy

L1: tiny + fastest (closest layer)

L2: bigger + slightly slower

L3: largest cache + slowest cache (often shared)

Why cache exists: it reduces latency by keeping likely-needed data close to the CPU (often using prefetching).

Multi-core vs Co-processors

Why do computers have both CPUs and GPUs?

Multi-core CPU: several general-purpose cores.

Great for running many different tasks (OS, apps, decision-heavy work).

Speed-up depends on how well software supports parallel processing.

GPU (a co-processor) has thousands of smaller cores.

Best when the same operation is applied to lots of data (graphics, matrix maths, ML).

Quick Check

🧠 Quick Check

Explain why a dual-core CPU is not always twice as fast as a single-core CPU.

Because: only the parallelisable part of a workload can run on both cores. Some tasks are sequential, and performance can be limited by memory/I/O bottlenecks.

From Instruction → Action

How does the CPU execute one instruction, step-by-step?

The CPU runs the fetch–decode–execute cycle.

Exam answers should include register transfers and buses.

Press Down for the stages

Stage 1: Fetch

1. PC → MAR (address of next instruction)

2. CU sends READ on the control bus

3. Instruction returns on the data bus into MDR

4. MDR → IR (current instruction ready to decode)

5. PC ← PC + 1 (ready for the next fetch)

Stage 2: Decode

The CU interprets the opcode in the IR.

It prepares control signals and identifies any operand addresses.

This is where the CPU decides: ALU operation? memory access? branch?

Stage 3: Execute

The CPU performs the operation (often in the ALU).

Results may be stored in a register (e.g., AC) or written back to memory.

Some instructions also update the PC (e.g., branches/jumps).

🧠 Quick Check

Which register holds the instruction currently being decoded/executed?

The IR (Instruction Register) holds the current instruction for the CU to decode.

HL Pipelining

How can a CPU increase throughput without making each stage “faster”?

Pipelining overlaps stages so multiple instructions are “in flight”.

Goal: increase throughput (instructions per cycle), not necessarily reduce single-instruction latency.

Assembly line analogy

Each stage does a different job (fetch, decode, execute…).

Once stage 1 finishes instruction A, it immediately starts instruction B.

Five-stage pipeline (common model)

Fetch → Decode → Execute → Memory → Write-back

Ideal case: close to 1 instruction per cycle once the pipeline is full.

Misconception Check

A. The address bus is typically bidirectional.

B. The PC stores the address of the next instruction to fetch.

C. A cache miss can stall the CPU while it waits for data.

D. A GPU is an example of a co-processor.

Press Down for answers

Answers

A: False. Address bus is usually CPU → memory (unidirectional).

B: True. PC points to the next instruction address.

C: True. A miss forces access to slower memory levels.

D: True. GPUs offload highly parallel tasks from the CPU.

Key Takeaways

  • CPU executes instructions using the fetch–decode–execute cycle.
  • Registers (PC, MAR, MDR, IR, AC) control addresses, instructions, and intermediate results.
  • Buses separate address, data, and control signals.
  • Memory hierarchy reduces stalls via cache (hits vs misses).
  • HL Pipelining increases throughput by overlapping stages.
